newsitem.title: BOSNIA: In chilly Sarajevo, no outcry over gas cut-off.
newsitem.headline: In chilly Sarajevo, no outcry over gas cut-off.

text.p: Freezing weather has sent a bitter chill through war-blasted Sarajevo where people have been without cooking and heating gas for the past two weeks, residents said on Tuesday.
A dispute over a $12.4 million owed to a Russian gas supplier has left Sarajevans shivering in wintry weather more than a year after their 43-month war ended.
Bosnia's Serb and Moslem-Croat federation officials have been quarreling over how to pay the debt, prompting the Russian gas company to cut off supplies on April 1.
International officials have urged the central government to pay now and settle the issue later for the sake of the city's 360,000 residents.

A major source of heating in Sarajevo, gas is a precious source of energy to almost every household. But instead of protesting, Sarajevans have sought alternatives to gas heating to stave off the cold.

"We continue to be concerned with the gas issue and frankly we are a little bit astonished that there isn't a more democratic outcry and complaint about the lack of gas," said Colum Murphy, spokesman for the international High Representative to Bosnia.

"I think it's the war psychology and it's also a legacy of the communist era...People just grit their teeth and say: 'Soon it'll be spring and summer and this is just another thing to bear at the moment,' instead of complaining," Murphy told Reuters.
"I'm afraid I have no influence over the issue," shrugged 22-year old Eldin. "It didn't even occur to me (to complain)."
Some Sarajevans say the city government, which is involved in the gas talks, is shirking its responsibilities.
"Yeah, I'd like to complain to our mayor, but we don't have one," said Mladen, 32.
The capital has been without a mayor for more than a year because Moslem and Croat politicians could not agree on the ethnic composition of the city government.
In the meantime, city residents have started to look for other sources of heating, buying electric heaters or rigging up wood-burning stoves.
"People are looking to remove gas as a source of energy and are trying to find alternatives instead of protesting and saying something is wrong with the system," an embittered lawyer said.
"They think: 'At least there is no shelling' and they submit themselves for more punishment," Darko, 37, said. "We lived better in some periods of war then we do now."
Besieged by Bosnian Serb forces from April 1992 until March 1996, Sarajevo went for months without electricity, water and gas as the Serbs turned utilities on and off at will.
Western envoys working to implement Bosnia's peace treaty said they hoped Bosnians would shrug off the numbing effects of war and eventually demand accountability from politicians.
"Surely the society we are all trying to improve and build here will one day be one where the system stands up to demand better service from their politicians," Murphy said.
